method: The oversubscription ratio is the combined line rate of the access ports divided by the combined line rate of the active uplink ports, both in the same unit and one direction: access capacity is the port count times the access port speed, uplink capacity is the active uplink count times the uplink port speed, and the ratio is the first divided by the second. Forty-eight 1 Gbps ports behind two 10 Gbps uplinks is 48 Gbps against 20 Gbps, or 2.4:1, which means the access ports cannot all send at full line rate through the uplinks at the same time. A ratio at or below 1:1 means the uplinks match or exceed the access capacity, so the boundary is not oversubscribed. The peak demand is the access capacity multiplied by the share of line rate expected at the busiest moment, the uplink load is that demand as a percentage of the uplink capacity, and the headroom is the uplink capacity minus the demand, so a negative headroom means the assumed peak cannot pass in one direction even though the design ratio looks normal. The uplink count a target ratio needs is the access capacity divided by the target ratio times the uplink speed, rounded up to a whole port, and the headroom against the target is the target ratio times the uplink capacity minus the access capacity. Only active, forwarding uplink members are counted: a standby or blocked bundle member adds no usable bandwidth. The ratio describes provisioned capacity, not measured throughput, queueing, latency, per-flow hashing or traffic that stays on the same switch, so it is a planning figure for one boundary rather than a design certification; common guidance allows roughly 20:1 at the access edge and about 4:1 at aggregation and core. Values are refused outside 1 to 4096 access ports, 1 to 256 uplink ports, 1% to 100% peak utilization and a 1:1 to 100:1 target, port speeds come from a fixed list of line rates, and decimal commas are accepted. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Oversubscription is expressed as the ratio of the bandwidth the access ports could demand to the bandwidth the uplink provides, so a 48-port 1 Gbps switch with one 10 Gbps uplink is 4.8:1.

Widely used planning guidance puts the access-to-distribution oversubscription ratio at no more than 20:1 and distribution-to-core at no more than 4:1, and advises monitoring uplink bandwidth before changing the ratio.
